theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a remuneration strategy in a public agency?
options: To pay every officer the same amount, whatever the job
To attract, keep and motivate the right staff fairly and within budget
To keep pay as low as possible whatever the effect on staffing
To match whatever the highest-paying private firm offers

questions.stem: A statutory body's strategic plan aims to build digital services. How should this affect its remuneration strategy?
options: It should not, as pay and strategy are separate matters for different units
It should freeze pay for all other staff to fund new posts in digital
It should help the body attract and keep scarce digital skills
It should pay digital staff by the hour so that they can be let go

questions.stem: Which list best describes 'total rewards'?
options: Basic salary and nothing else that the employer provides
Overtime pay and any bonus paid at the end of the year
Only the allowances that are added to each officer's pay slip every month
Pay, benefits, development, recognition and working conditions

questions.stem: An officer earns a basic salary of J$3,000,000 a year, J$360,000 in allowances, and the agency pays J$240,000 a year for her health insurance. What is the value of this package?
Two officers in a ministry do jobs of the same size and demands, but one is paid much more because she 'negotiated well' when hired. Which principle is at risk?
options: External competitiveness with the private sector
Internal equity between jobs of equal value
Value for money in the purchase of supplies
The separation of duties in the payment process

questions.stem: What does job evaluation measure?
options: How well each person is performing in their present job this year
How long each person has worked for the organisation in total
The relative size or value of each job, not the person in it
How much each person would be paid by a competing employer

questions.stem: A point-factor scheme scores jobs on factors such as knowledge, problem-solving, responsibility and working conditions. What is its main advantage?
options: It needs no job descriptions or trained evaluators to run it
It lets the most senior manager rank the jobs by personal view
It ties every job's pay to the market rate automatically
It gives a consistent, explainable basis for comparing jobs

questions.stem: Grade 4 covers 350 to 449 points and Grade 5 covers 450 to 549 points. A job is evaluated at 420 points. In which grade does it belong?
options: Grade 4
Grade 5
Grade 3
Between grades 4 and 5

questions.stem: Before a job is evaluated, what must be in place?
options: The present jobholder's latest appraisal rating and file
An accurate, current job description agreed with the manager
The salary the jobholder would like to be paid next year
A pay survey showing what other agencies pay for the post

questions.stem: An agency keeps losing accountants to private firms. What is the best first step in reviewing their pay?
options: Give every accountant an increase of 20% at once
Ask the accountants who have left to name what they think a fair salary is
Compare its pay with reliable survey data for similar jobs
Stop recruiting accountants and use temporary staff

questions.stem: A salary survey shows a median of J$3,200,000 for a job. The agency pays J$2,880,000. Where is the agency's pay?
options: 10% above the market median
At the market median
11% above the market median
10% below the market median

questions.stem: What is a 'benchmark job' in a salary survey?
options: A common job, clearly defined, that can be matched across employers
The highest-paid job in the organisation, used as the top limit for all pay
A job that has been empty for more than six months
A job that the survey firm itself has created for testing

questions.stem: An agency decides to pay at the 75th percentile of the market for scarce IT jobs and at the median for others. What is this approach called?
options: A pay freeze across the whole organisation
Setting different market positions for different job groups
Paying everyone at the lowest point the law allows
Paying only for long service, with no link at all to the market rates

questions.stem: What does paying at the median of the market mean?
options: Paying more than every other employer in the survey
Paying the average of the highest and lowest rates seen
Half of the surveyed rates are higher and half are lower
Paying the rate that the largest employer in the survey pays

questions.stem: A pay range runs from J$2,000,000 to J$3,000,000. What is its midpoint?
The same range runs from J$2,000,000 to J$3,000,000. What is its range spread, measured as (maximum − minimum) ÷ minimum?
Why do pay ranges for neighbouring grades often overlap?
options: To make sure that every officer in a grade is paid the same
So an experienced officer in a lower grade can earn more than a newcomer in the next
To hide the true size of each grade from the staff
Because job evaluation cannot tell the grades apart

questions.stem: An agency replaces 14 narrow grades with 5 wide pay bands. What is this called?
options: Job enrichment
Red-circling
Broadbanding
Benchmarking

questions.stem: An officer earns J$2,640,000. The midpoint of her range is J$2,400,000. What is her compa-ratio?
Most officers in one grade have compa-ratios of about 85%, while the market has moved up. What does this suggest?
options: They are paid well below the midpoint, which may hurt retention
They are paid well above the midpoint, and their pay should now be frozen
They are paid exactly at the market rate for their grade
The grade has too many officers and should be cut

questions.stem: After a new structure is introduced, an officer's present salary is above the maximum of his new grade. What is the usual approach?
options: Cut his salary to the new maximum from the next month
Protect his salary for a set period, with no increases until the range catches up
Move him to a higher grade even though the job is the same
Pay him the difference as a one-off bonus and then cut it

questions.stem: An officer is paid below the minimum of the grade her job has been evaluated into. What is this called, and what should happen?
options: A red circle; her pay is frozen until she leaves
A broadband; she should be moved into a lower grade
A green circle; her pay should be raised to the minimum, often in steps
A benchmark; her pay should be used to set the range

questions.stem: In a service-based scale, how does an officer usually move up the range?
options: By asking the manager for a raise when she feels it is due
By a bonus that is paid only in years when the agency makes a surplus or profit
By a points score from the latest job evaluation exercise
By set increments, usually yearly, subject to satisfactory work

questions.stem: A ministry plans to link part of pay to performance. What must be in place first for this to be fair?
options: A sound, trusted appraisal system with clear targets
A pay range with no maximum, so rewards have no limit
Agreement from the best performers only
A promise that every officer will receive the top award

questions.stem: What is a common risk of individual performance-related pay in teams that depend on each other?
options: Staff work together too closely and lose their own skills
It can weaken teamwork and encourage staff to compete
The pay bill always falls sharply in the first year
It removes the need for managers to give any feedback

questions.stem: An officer earning J$2,000,000 receives a merit increase of 5%. What is the new salary?
Officers who use their own cars for field visits receive a travel allowance. What should the remuneration plan make clear about it?
options: That any officer may claim it whether or not they travel
That it replaces the officers' basic salary for those months
That it is paid only to officers in the most senior grades
Who qualifies, the rate, how it is reviewed and what records are needed

questions.stem: A parish council cannot raise pay this year. Which action is most likely to help keep good staff?
options: Offer development, flexible working and recognition for good work
Tell staff that any complaints about pay will be noted on their personal files
Remove the yearly increments without explanation
Announce that no posts will be filled for two years

questions.stem: What do the minimum wage law and the equal pay law mainly require of an employer?
options: That all staff in the same grade are paid exactly the same amount
A wage at or above the legal minimum, and equal pay for women and men in equal work
That every salary is published in the newspaper each year
That pay rises match the rise in prices every year

questions.stem: When a remuneration plan is costed, why must statutory deductions and employer contributions be considered?
options: Because they can be waived for staff in the public sector
Because they are paid only by staff who earn bonuses
Because the law requires them and employer contributions add to the cost
Because they replace the need for a pension scheme

questions.stem: Men in a grade earn an average of J$2,500,000 and women in the same grade earn J$2,200,000. What is the gap, as a percentage of men's pay?
A pay audit finds the gap in the previous question. What should the HR manager do first?
options: Find the reasons, such as starting pay or grading, and check them for fairness
Cut the men's salaries so that the averages match
Close the audit, as small differences are normal
Publish the names and salaries of all officers in the grade

questions.stem: An agency has 120 staff with an average salary of J$2,500,000. A 4% increase is proposed. What is the yearly cost of the increase, before employer contributions?
Why should the cost of a pay award be worked out for future years, not only the first year?
options: Because pay awards are paid only once and then removed
Because the auditors never look at the first year's costs
Because a raise to basic pay carries forward and affects other pay-linked costs
Because staff numbers always fall in later years

questions.stem: A proposed new pay structure would cost more than the agency's approved budget for salaries. What should the HR manager do?
options: Introduce it anyway and ask for extra money later
Introduce it only for the HR department first
Hide the extra cost under another budget line
Phase it in or adjust it so that it is affordable, and get the needed approvals

questions.stem: Staff in a statutory body are represented by a union. A new pay structure is planned. What should management do?
options: Consult and negotiate with the union as the agreements and law require
Announce the new structure to staff on the day that it comes into effect
Speak only to staff who are not union members
Wait for the union to find out and complain

questions.stem: Why can a public agency not usually set its own pay scales freely, as a private firm can?
options: Because public officers are not allowed to be paid allowances
Because pay is set within central government policy and approvals, and the budget
Because public pay is decided by the officers themselves
Because private firms set the pay of public officers

questions.stem: A new pay structure has been approved. What should each officer be told?
options: Nothing, as pay matters are confidential to HR
Only the new salaries of the senior managers, so staff can see the top of the scale
How the structure works, their own grade and pay, and how to appeal
The salaries of everyone else in their grade

questions.stem: An officer believes her job has been placed in the wrong grade. What should the remuneration plan provide?
options: No route to challenge, so that the structure stays fixed
A promise that every challenge will succeed
A rule that challenges are decided by her colleagues
A clear review or appeal process with set time limits

questions.stem: A manager asks HR for a spreadsheet of all salaries in the agency 'to get a feel for the numbers'. What should the HR manager do?
options: Share only the data he needs for his role, in line with data protection rules
Send the full file, as all managers may see all salaries
Post the file on the shared drive for everyone
Refuse to give any information to any manager

questions.stem: Which evidence best shows whether a remuneration strategy is helping an agency keep staff?
options: The number of pages in the remuneration policy and its appendices
Turnover, exit interview reasons and time to fill posts
How many staff attended the pay briefing
The cost of printing the new pay scales

questions.stem: 24 officers left an agency during the year. The average number employed was 160. What was the turnover rate?
When should an agency review its remuneration strategy?
options: Only when staff go on strike
Every ten years, when a new survey is done
Never, once it has been approved
Regularly, such as yearly, and when markets or plans change

questions.stem: A new structure is to start on 1 April. Which step best avoids pay errors?
options: Check each officer's new grade and pay before the first payroll run
Let officers report any errors in their new pay after they have been paid
Run the old and new payrolls at random for a month
Ask payroll to work out the new pay as they see fit

questions.stem: A director asks the HR manager to grade his niece's new post higher than its evaluation shows. What should the HR manager do?
options: Agree, as directors may decide the grades of new posts
Refuse, keep to the evaluation, and report the request under the code of conduct
Agree, but only for the first year of the niece's contract
Split the difference and place the post one grade higher

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term names the systematic process of judging the relative size of jobs to build a fair grading structure?
What term names an officer's salary divided by the midpoint of their pay range?
What term names the middle point of a pay range, usually set at the market rate for a fully competent officer?
The midpoint of a range is J$2,200,000. An officer's compa-ratio is 95%. What is her salary, in J$?
What two-word term names the full package of pay, benefits, development, recognition and working conditions an employer offers?
What term names the protection of an officer whose salary is above the maximum of their new grade? (Hyphenated, or two words.)
What two-word term names the study of what other employers pay for similar jobs?
What one-word term names replacing many narrow grades with a few wide pay bands?
A travel allowance is J$25,000 a month. What is it worth over a year, in J$?
Which statistic in a salary survey is the middle value, with half the rates above it and half below?
A pay bill of J$80,000,000 rises by 3%. What is the cost of the increase, in J$?
What one-word term names the fixed step by which an officer's pay rises within a scale, usually each year?
What two-word term names the negotiation of pay and conditions between an employer and a union on behalf of staff?
An agency employs 200 staff on average and wants yearly turnover of no more than 10%. What is the largest number of leavers in a year that meets this target?
What two-word term names fairness in pay between jobs of similar value inside the same organisation?

essays.stem: Explain what a remuneration strategy for a public agency should contain, and how it should link to the agency's strategic plan.
essays.modelAnswer: A remuneration strategy sets out how the agency will reward staff to deliver its plan. It should begin with its aims: to attract, keep and motivate people with the skills the plan needs, to pay fairly between jobs and between women and men, and to stay within the approved salary budget and central government's pay policy. It should state the agency's market position, for example the median for most jobs and a higher point for scarce skills such as IT. It should describe the pay structure, how jobs are graded through job evaluation, how pay moves within ranges, and the place of allowances, benefits and non-financial rewards. It should say how pay will be reviewed, costed and approved, how staff and unions will be consulted, and how decisions are communicated and appealed. Finally, it should set measures of success, such as turnover, time to fill posts and pay equity results. The link to the strategic plan is direct: if the plan needs new skills or better service, the strategy must direct reward to those priorities.
markingPoints: States aims: attract, retain, motivate, fairness, affordability within policy
States market position and pay structure, linked to job evaluation
Covers progression, benefits and non-financial rewards
Covers review, costing, approval, consultation and appeals
Links clearly to the strategic plan and sets measures of success

essays.stem: Describe how you would run a job evaluation exercise in an agency of 150 staff, and explain how you would keep it fair.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by agreeing the purpose and the scheme with senior management and the union, choosing an analytical point-factor scheme so that results can be explained. I would set up a trained panel with members from different departments, men and women, and a union observer. Each job would need an accurate, current job description, checked by the jobholder and manager, because the job is evaluated, not the person. The panel would score each job on the agreed factors, such as knowledge, problem-solving, responsibility, contacts and working conditions, by consensus, and record the reasons. I would first evaluate a set of benchmark jobs to test the scheme. After all jobs are scored, I would rank them, draw grade boundaries at natural gaps in the points, and check the results for oddities and for any pattern that disadvantages women or one group. Officers would be told the outcome and given a clear appeal process. Fairness comes from consistent factors, trained evaluators, recorded reasons, equality checks, openness and appeals.
markingPoints: Agrees purpose and an analytical scheme, with consultation
Trained, balanced panel and accurate job descriptions
Scores jobs on factors, evaluating the job not the person, with recorded reasons
Tests with benchmark jobs, ranks and sets grade boundaries, and checks for bias
Communicates results with an appeal process

essays.stem: Grade 6 has a range of J$2,000,000 to J$3,000,000. Three officers earn J$2,200,000, J$2,500,000 and J$2,900,000. Work out each compa-ratio and explain what the results tell the HR manager.
essays.modelAnswer: The midpoint is (J$2,000,000 + J$3,000,000) ÷ 2 = J$2,500,000. The compa-ratios are: J$2,200,000 ÷ J$2,500,000 = 88%; J$2,500,000 ÷ J$2,500,000 = 100%; and J$2,900,000 ÷ J$2,500,000 = 116%. The first officer is paid 12% below the midpoint. If she is new to the job this is normal, but if she is experienced and performing well, she may be underpaid and at risk of leaving. The second is paid exactly at the midpoint, the rate usually set for a fully competent officer. The third is 16% above the midpoint and close to the range maximum, which suits a long-serving, high-performing officer but leaves little room for future increases. The HR manager should check each result against experience, performance and the market, look for patterns such as gender differences, and use the findings to plan increases: larger steps for well-performing officers low in the range, and smaller steps near the top.
markingPoints: Midpoint J$2,500,000 correct
Compa-ratios 88%, 100% and 116% correct
Interprets low, midpoint and high positions
Checks results against experience, performance, market and equity
Uses results to guide future increases

essays.stem: An agency is losing IT staff to private firms, but its pay must stay within public pay policy. Evaluate the options and recommend a remuneration response.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would confirm the problem with evidence: turnover and exit interviews for IT staff, and a reliable salary survey showing how far our pay lags the market. One option is to raise IT salaries to the market median or above. This targets the problem but may break internal equity and need central approval, and it costs money every year. A second option is a market or scarce-skills allowance for named IT jobs, reviewed each year. This can be easier to approve and remove, but it must have clear rules so other groups see it as fair. A third is to improve non-pay rewards: training and certification, flexible and remote working, modern equipment and clear career paths, which matter greatly to IT staff and cost less. A fourth is a retention payment tied to staying a set time. I recommend a reviewed scarce-skills allowance, approved under the rules, combined with stronger development and flexible working, with turnover measured over the next year.
markingPoints: Confirms the problem with turnover, exit data and survey evidence
Evaluates raising salaries (targeted but costly, equity and approval issues)
Evaluates a scarce-skills or market allowance with clear rules
Evaluates non-pay rewards and retention payments
Gives a justified recommendation within policy, with measures

essays.stem: Compare service-based increments with performance-related pay for a public body, and recommend which it should use.
essays.modelAnswer: Service-based increments move officers up the scale each year if their work is satisfactory. They are simple to run, predictable for budgets and staff, and seen as fair because the rules are the same for all. However, they reward time served rather than results, and a poor performer reaches the top of the range as fast as a strong one. Performance-related pay links increases to appraisal results. It can reward and keep the best performers and signal what the body values. Its success depends on a trusted appraisal system with clear targets and trained managers; without that, it can seem biased, cause disputes, weaken teamwork and cost more to administer. In public bodies, where results are often shared and hard to measure for one person, these risks are real. I would recommend keeping increments, but making them depend on a satisfactory appraisal, and adding a modest, team-based or individual award for outstanding performance once the appraisal system is shown to be sound.
markingPoints: Explains increments: simple, predictable, seen as fair, but reward service
Explains performance pay: rewards results, signals values
Notes the conditions and risks of performance pay (appraisal, bias, teamwork, cost)
Relates the comparison to a public body's setting
Gives a justified recommendation

essays.stem: An agency has 120 staff with an average salary of J$2,500,000. Management proposes a 4% pay increase. Work out the cost and explain everything else that must be considered before it is approved.
essays.modelAnswer: The pay bill is 120 × J$2,500,000 = J$300,000,000. A 4% increase costs J$300,000,000 × 4% = J$12,000,000 a year in basic pay. That is not the full cost. Employer contributions that rise with pay must be added at the current rates, and so must any pension costs and allowances or overtime rates that are linked to basic pay. Because the increase is built into basic pay, it carries into every future year and raises the base for later increases. I would check whether the amount fits the approved salary budget and central pay policy, and whether approval from the parent ministry or finance ministry is needed. I would consider timing: an increase from mid-year costs only part of the amount in the first year. I would look at whether a flat percentage is the fairest choice, or whether officers low in their ranges or in scarce jobs need more. Finally, I would plan consultation with the union and how the decision will be communicated.
markingPoints: Pay bill J$300,000,000 and increase J$12,000,000 correct
Adds pay-linked costs such as employer contributions at current rates and pensions
Notes the cost carries forward into future years
Checks budget, policy and approvals, and the timing effect
Considers fairness of a flat increase, consultation and communication

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a pay equity review in a ministry, and what you would do with the results.
essays.modelAnswer: I would gather pay data for every officer: grade, salary, allowances, start date, performance rating and gender, kept secure under the data protection law and analysed by a small authorised team. I would compare the average and median pay of women and men in each grade and in jobs of equal value, and also look at other groups where data allows. Where gaps appear, I would find the causes: starting salaries agreed case by case, faster progression for some groups, allowances given unevenly, or jobs mainly done by women graded too low. Each cause would be judged on whether it can be justified on fair grounds such as length of service. Unjustified gaps would be corrected through a costed plan, such as raising pay in steps, regrading jobs after evaluation, and setting clear rules for starting pay and allowances. I would report the findings and actions to senior management, inform staff in general terms without naming anyone, and repeat the review each year to track progress.
markingPoints: Gathers complete pay data securely, under data protection
Compares pay by gender within grades and jobs of equal value
Investigates causes and tests whether each is justified
Corrects unjustified gaps with a costed plan and clear rules
Reports, communicates without naming individuals, and repeats the review

essays.stem: A new pay structure has been approved for a statutory body. Plan how you would put it into practice.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set a start date that gives payroll time to prepare, and confirm the budget and approvals in writing. I would then place each officer into the new structure: find their new grade from the job evaluation and decide where they sit in the range under agreed rules. Officers below their new minimum would be raised, possibly in steps, and those above their new maximum would have their pay protected for a set period. I would prepare a letter for each officer stating their grade, pay, how they will progress and how to appeal. Managers would be briefed first so they can answer questions, and the union kept involved. I would hold staff sessions explaining how the structure works. Payroll would check every new rate before the first run, with a second person checking a sample. I would open an appeals process with time limits. After three and twelve months I would review appeals, costs, turnover and staff views, and report the results to the board.
markingPoints: Confirms budget, approvals and a realistic start date
Places officers using agreed rules, including below-minimum and above-maximum cases
Individual letters, manager briefings, union involvement and staff sessions
Checks payroll accuracy before the first run
Runs appeals and reviews results after implementation

essays.stem: Justify why non-financial rewards matter in a public-sector remuneration plan, and recommend which a parish council should use when it cannot raise pay.
essays.modelAnswer: Pay matters, but it is not the only reason people join, stay and work hard. Research and exit interviews often show that people leave because of poor management, no development, unfair treatment or inflexible hours, not only pay. In the public sector, where pay rises are limited by budgets and central policy, non-financial rewards are one of the few tools a manager controls, and many cost little. They also support a sense of public service, which motivates many officers. A parish council that cannot raise pay should first ask staff what they value, through a short survey. I would then recommend: training and study support that lead to qualifications and promotion; clear career paths and acting opportunities; flexible start times or compressed hours where service allows; regular recognition, such as thanks from the council and staff awards; better equipment and working conditions; and wellbeing support. These should be applied fairly, with clear rules, and their effect checked through turnover and staff surveys.
markingPoints: Explains why non-financial rewards affect retention and motivation
Links to limits on public-sector pay and public service motivation
Finds out what staff value
Recommends specific, suitable rewards for a parish council
Applies them fairly and measures their effect

essays.stem: Explain how you would evaluate whether an agency's remuneration strategy is working, and how the findings should shape the next pay review.
essays.modelAnswer: I would measure the strategy against its aims. For attracting staff, I would track time to fill posts, the number and quality of applicants and offers refused because of pay. For keeping staff, I would track turnover, especially among high performers and scarce skills, and the reasons given in exit interviews. For motivation and fairness, I would use staff survey results on pay and recognition, the number of grading appeals and grievances, and a pay equity review by gender. For affordability, I would compare the actual pay bill with the budget and the plan. I would also compare our pay with up-to-date survey data and check compa-ratios to see how officers sit in their ranges. I would report the findings to senior management with clear conclusions. The next pay review should then target the problems found: for example, more for scarce skills if those officers are leaving, correcting unfair gaps, adjusting ranges if many staff are low in them, and improving non-pay rewards that staff value, all within the budget.
markingPoints: Measures attraction: time to fill, applicants, refused offers
Measures retention: turnover and exit reasons
Measures fairness and motivation: surveys, appeals, pay equity
Measures affordability and market position (pay bill, surveys, compa-ratios)
Uses findings to target the next pay review within budget

practical1.title: Evaluate and grade a set of jobs and propose pay ranges
practical1.brief: Your group is the job evaluation panel of a public agency. The assessor gives you six short job descriptions, a simple point-factor scheme (factors, levels and points) and salary survey data for three of the jobs. First, score each job on each factor, agreeing the score as a panel and recording the reason. Then rank the jobs, draw grade boundaries and place each job in a grade. Finally, use the survey data to propose a minimum, midpoint and maximum for each grade, and write a half-page note explaining the structure. Give each member a named role: panel chair (keeps the process fair and the panel on time), recorder (keeps the scoring sheet and the reasons), analyst (adds the points and builds the ranking in a spreadsheet or on paper), market analyst (works out the ranges from the survey data), and in a group of five an equality checker (checks the scores and grades for bias). Present the structure to the assessor, with every member explaining their part.
materials: Assessor's pack: six job descriptions, point-factor scheme and survey data
Scoring sheets and a grade structure template
Computer with spreadsheet, or paper and calculators
photos: The scoring sheet with factor scores and reasons for each job
The ranking of jobs by total points
The grade boundaries and the job placed in each grade
The proposed pay ranges with the working shown
The explanatory note and the group presenting to the assessor
checklist: Carried out a named role and produced their own part of the evidence
Scored jobs on the job content, not on the jobholder, and recorded reasons
Added points correctly and ranked the jobs accurately
Set sensible grade boundaries and placed every job
Worked out ranges and midpoints correctly from the survey data
Checked the results for bias and explained any changes
Explained their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Use only the made-up job descriptions and figures in the pack
Keep all pay data confidential and collect every copy at the end
Disagree with scores politely and decide by discussion, not pressure
Take short breaks and share the workload fairly

practical2.title: Cost a yearly pay review and present it to the HR committee
practical2.brief: Your group is the HR team of a statutory body. The assessor gives you a staff list of about 20 posts (grade, salary, range, performance rating and gender), the salary budget for next year and two options from management: a flat 4% increase for all, or a targeted increase that gives more to officers low in their ranges and to scarce skills. Work out the cost of each option, each officer's compa-ratio before and after, and any pay equity issues. Then write a two-page recommendation and present it to a role-played HR committee, with the assessor as chair and one member as the union representative. Give each member a named role: team lead, costing analyst (works out both options), compa-ratio and equity analyst, report writer, and in a group of five the union representative. Every member must speak in the committee meeting. Photograph each stage.
materials: Assessor's pack: staff list, ranges, budget and the two options
Computer with spreadsheet and printer, or paper and calculators
photos: The spreadsheet or working sheet costing both options
The compa-ratio table before and after each option
checklist: Carried out a named role and contributed to the evidence
Cost of each option worked out correctly and compared with the budget
Compa-ratios worked out correctly and used to support the recommendation
Identified pay equity issues and proposed fair action
Recommendation is clear, affordable and justified
Spoke professionally in the committee and responded to the union's points
Kept individual pay data confidential throughout
safety: Use only the made-up staff list; no real names or salaries
Keep the spreadsheet in the Centre's shared folder and delete copies from personal devices
Keep the committee role play respectful, including the union discussion
Share the workload fairly and take a screen break each hour
